title: Haaretz: Hostage Families Became a Political Force After Oct. 7 — but Not a Monolith, and Not an Easy Fit for the Opposition
detail: Haaretz reported Monday, September 14, 2026 that hostage and bereaved families — who became some of Israel's most visible political figures through their post-October 7 activism — have struggled to translate that visibility into a clear role within opposition parties ahead of the October 27 election, despite opposition politicians having long championed their campaign against the government. The article noted that hostage families were 'never a political monolith': most relatives pushed for ceasefire deals to bring captives home even at the cost of ending military operations, while a smaller group backed continued pressure on Hamas and aligned with the government. It cited Talik Gvili, a hostage family member who appeared at a Likud Knesset slate announcement crediting Prime Minister Netanyahu with bringing home all the hostages, including her son, as an example of how family members have been claimed across the political spectrum rather than uniformly absorbed by the opposition bloc that amplified their protests. The piece is part of a broader Haaretz elections-desk pattern documenting how October 7 accountability and the hostage crisis continue to shape campaign positioning as the third anniversary of the attack approaches.
